events.title: Vitellius proclaimed by the Rhine legions
events.summary: On 1 January 69 the legions IV Macedonica and XXII Primigenia at Mogontiacum overturned Galba's images and refused the oath; the next day Fabius Valens led the lower German army at Cologne to hail its governor, Aulus Vitellius, as emperor. The upper army joined on 3 January.
events.detail: The Rhine legions resented Galba's failure to reward them for crushing Vindex and his dismissal of Verginius Rufus. Vitellius, a gourmand appointed by Galba as harmless, took the name Germanicus but refused that of Caesar at first. Two columns under Valens and Caecina marched on Italy while Vitellius followed with reserves.

events.title: Murder of Galba
events.summary: Five days after Galba adopted the aristocrat Lucius Calpurnius Piso Licinianus, Marcus Salvius Otho, passed over and in debt, was carried to the praetorian camp by 23 bodyguards and hailed emperor. Galba was cut down in the Forum near the Lacus Curtius, and Piso was dragged from the temple of Vesta and killed.
events.detail: Galba had alienated the praetorians by refusing the donative promised in his name, declaring that he 'chose his soldiers, he did not buy them'. Tacitus's epitaph is famous: 'by universal consent capable of ruling, had he not ruled' (capax imperii nisi imperasset). Galba's adoption speech in Tacitus (Hist. 1.15-16), presenting adoption of the best man as a substitute for liberty, anticipates the ideology of the adoptive emperors under whom Tacitus wrote.

events.title: First Battle of Bedriacum
events.summary: Otho's generals, ordered to force a decision against the advice of Suetonius Paullinus and Marius Celsus, advanced from Bedriacum towards Cremona and were defeated in a confused battle along the Via Postumia by the combined Vitellian armies of Caecina and Valens.
events.detail: Otho remained at Brixellum with part of his forces, a decision Tacitus blames. The Danubian legions marching to Otho's aid had not arrived. The battle was fought among vines and ditches; legio I Adiutrix (Otho's marines) captured the eagle of XXI Rapax but was then routed. Many Othonian survivors were sent back to their Danube bases, where they soon declared for Vespasian.

battle.significance: Decided the war between Otho and Vitellius; Otho killed himself two days later.

events.title: Suicide of Otho
events.summary: Though his army was still largely intact and the Danube legions were coming, Otho decided to spare Rome further civil war; he burned compromising letters, distributed money, slept soundly and at dawn stabbed himself at Brixellum, aged 37. Several soldiers killed themselves at his pyre.
events.detail: Ancient writers who despised his life as Nero's companion admired his death: Martial (6.32) says Cato's death was less glorious than Otho's. Tacitus records that he had reigned 95 days. The episode became a classic exemplum of a noble end.

events.title: Vespasian proclaimed emperor at Alexandria
events.summary: On 1 July 69 Tiberius Julius Alexander, prefect of Egypt, had his legions swear allegiance to Titus Flavius Vespasianus, commander in the Jewish war; the army of Judaea followed on 3 July and Mucianus's Syrian legions soon after. Vespasian later counted his reign from 1 July.
events.detail: The plan was coordinated with Mucianus, governor of Syria, who led an army west while Vespasian held Egypt to control Rome's grain. At Alexandria Vespasian reportedly healed a blind man and a man with a crippled hand at Serapis's urging, miracles that gave the new dynasty divine sanction; Tacitus says eyewitnesses still vouched for them when there was nothing to gain by lying. Josephus's prophecy at Jotapata was recalled, and he was freed.

events.title: Second Battle of Bedriacum and sack of Cremona
events.summary: Antonius Primus's Danubian army met the leaderless Vitellian legions (Caecina had tried to defect and been arrested by his own men) in a night battle before Cremona. At dawn legio III Gallica saluted the rising sun in Syrian fashion, the Vitellians thought reinforcements had come, and broke. The Flavians then sacked Cremona for four days.
events.detail: Tacitus tells of a son who killed his father in the battle and recognised him while stripping the body. Some 40,000 soldiers and camp followers poured into Cremona, which was burned to the ground except for a temple of Mefitis; Dio gives 50,000 dead in the battle and sack. Augustus's colony took years to rebuild. The battle opened Italy to the Flavians.
events.locName: Before Cremona on the Via Postumia

sides.strength: Five Danubian legions and auxiliaries, c. 30,000-40,000

battle.significance: Decisive Flavian victory of the civil war.

events.title: Burning of the Capitol
events.summary: After Vitellius's agreement to abdicate was blocked by his soldiers and the city mob, Vespasian's brother Flavius Sabinus, prefect of the city, took refuge on the Capitol with the young Domitian. Vitellian troops stormed it; the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus burned, and Sabinus was killed.
events.detail: Tacitus calls it the most lamentable and shameful crime in Rome's history: the temple founded under the kings, which neither Porsenna nor the Gauls had violated, destroyed by the madness of emperors. Domitian escaped disguised as an Isiac worshipper. Druids in Gaul, Tacitus says, saw in the burning a sign that world rule was passing to the peoples beyond the Alps. Vespasian began rebuilding in 70, personally carrying the first basket of rubble.

battle.significance: Destroyed Rome's chief temple; led to the Flavian storming of the city next day.

events.title: Flavian storming of Rome and death of Vitellius
events.summary: Antonius Primus's troops fought their way into Rome against the Vitellian praetorians while crowds watched and cheered as at a show. Vitellius, found hiding in a doorkeeper's lodge, was dragged half-naked through the Forum, pelted with dung and killed at the Gemonian stairs.
events.detail: Tacitus describes the city as simultaneously given over to slaughter and to the Saturnalia. The praetorian camp fell after desperate resistance. Mucianus arrived soon after and took control, sidelining Primus; Domitian, as Caesar, represented the family until Vespasian reached Rome in October 70.

events.title: Lex de imperio Vespasiani
events.summary: The Senate's decree of late December 69, confirmed by the people, conferring 'all the usual powers' on Vespasian survives in part on a bronze tablet in the Capitoline Museums. Its clauses grant powers 'as Augustus, Tiberius and Claudius had', omitting Caligula and Nero.
events.detail: The surviving portion lists rights to make treaties, convene and preside over the Senate, commend candidates, extend the pomerium, and a sweeping discretionary clause empowering him to do whatever he judges to be in the interests of the state; a final sanction validates all his acts before the law was passed (from his dies imperii, 1 July 69). The tablet was rediscovered by Cola di Rienzo, who used it in 1347 to argue for the sovereignty of the Roman people (CIL VI 930 = ILS 244). Brunt argued it was a standard enactment repeated for each emperor; others see novel features reflecting Vespasian's need for legitimacy.
scholarship: Brunt, 'Lex de imperio Vespasiani', JRS 67 (1977)
Capogrossi Colognesi and Gabba (eds), Gli statuti municipali / La Lex de imperio Vespasiani (2009)
events.debate: Standard formula or innovation; whether it was a lex or a senatus consultum ratified by the comitia.

events.title: Siege of Vetera
events.summary: Julius Civilis's Batavians and Germans besieged the double-legion fortress of Vetera, held by some 5,000 men of V Alaudae and XV Primigenia under Munius Lupercus, from autumn 69. After eating their horses and roots, the defenders surrendered in March 70 and were massacred five miles from the camp.
events.detail: Civilis had siege towers built by Roman deserters and prisoners; the defenders burned them with fire-darts and grapnels. A relief by Dillius Vocula briefly broke the siege in late 69. Lupercus was sent as a gift to the seeress Veleda but was killed on the way. Tacitus highlights the shame of legions surrendering to auxiliaries trained in Roman ways.

sides.strength: Eight Batavian veteran cohorts, Germanic allies
c. 5,000 of V Alaudae and XV Primigenia

battle.significance: The greatest humiliation of Roman arms on the Rhine since Varus.

events.title: Proclamation of the Imperium Galliarum
events.summary: Julius Classicus and Julius Tutor of the Treveri and Julius Sabinus of the Lingones, all Roman officers, proclaimed an 'Empire of the Gauls'. The legions at Novaesium and Bonna, after murdering their commander Dillius Vocula, swore allegiance to it; but a council of Gallic states at Durocortorum, convened by the Remi, chose loyalty to Rome.
events.detail: Sabinus, who claimed descent from Julius Caesar, was defeated by the Sequani, hid for nine years in a tomb with his wife Epponina, who bore two children there, and was executed in 79 despite her pleas, a story told by Plutarch and Dio. The episode showed the limits of Gallic separatism a century after the conquest: the provincial elites were too invested in Rome.

events.title: Battle of Rigodulum
events.summary: Quintus Petillius Cerialis, arriving with fresh legions from Italy, stormed the fortified Treveran position at Rigodulum on the Moselle, capturing its commander Julius Valentinus, and entered Augusta Treverorum the next day.
events.detail: At Trier Cerialis addressed the Treveri and Lingones in a speech that Tacitus made into the classic Roman justification of empire: Gaul had always had kings and wars until it accepted Roman rule; peace requires armies, armies pay, pay requires tribute; if Rome were expelled, nothing would follow but wars among all nations. Days later Civilis and Classicus surprised Cerialis's camp at Trier; he rallied his troops, half-dressed, and won.

sides.strength: Legio XXI Rapax, auxiliaries and new legions from Italy

events.title: Second battle of Vetera
events.summary: Civilis made his last stand near the ruins of Vetera, flooding the plain with a dam. After an inconclusive first day, a Batavian deserter guided Roman cavalry to the rear of the German line on the second, and Civilis was defeated.
events.detail: Civilis retreated to the Insula Batavorum, breaking Drusus's mole to flood the land. Cerialis negotiated, and Tacitus's account breaks off with Civilis addressing the Roman commander on a broken bridge over the Nabalia. The Batavi kept their privileged status and continued to supply elite cohorts, including those at Vindolanda a generation later.

sides.strength: Legions II Adiutrix, VI Victrix, XIV Gemina, XXI Rapax and auxiliaries

events.title: Siege and destruction of Jerusalem
events.summary: Titus besieged Jerusalem from Passover 70 with four legions and allied troops. Breaching the third and second walls in May, he encircled the city with a wall to starve it, took the Antonia fortress in July, burned the Temple at the end of August and stormed the Upper City in late September.
events.detail: The defenders were split among factions: John of Gischala held the Temple, Simon bar Giora the Upper City, and the Zealots of Eleazar ben Simon the inner courts until John seized them at Passover; they had burned each other's grain stores. Josephus, shouting appeals from outside the walls, describes famine so severe that a woman ate her child. The daily sacrifice ceased on 17 Panemos; the Temple burned on 10 Loos (Jewish tradition: 9 Av). Josephus claims Titus tried to save the Temple; Sulpicius Severus, probably drawing on a lost part of Tacitus, says Titus decided to destroy it to uproot both Jewish and Christian religion. Josephus's toll of 1,100,000 dead and 97,000 captives is impossible but reflects a catastrophe. Archaeology includes the 'Burnt House' with a spear and a young woman's arm bones, and Herodian street paving crushed by masonry thrown down from the Temple Mount.

sides.strength: Legions V Macedonica, X Fretensis, XII Fulminata, XV Apollinaris, auxiliaries and allied kings: c. 60,000-70,000
c. 23,000 fighters (Josephus) and a population swollen by Passover pilgrims
sides.losses: catastrophic; Josephus claims 1.1 million dead and 97,000 enslaved

battle.significance: Destroyed the Second Temple, ending sacrificial Judaism and reshaping both rabbinic Judaism and early Christianity.

scholarship: Goodman, Rome and Jerusalem (2007)
Rajak, Josephus: The Historian and His Society (2nd ed. 2002)
events.debate: Titus's intention regarding the Temple (Josephus vs Sulpicius Severus/Tacitus); casualty figures.

events.title: Institution of the fiscus Judaicus
events.summary: Vespasian ordered that the half-shekel Temple tax paid by Jews everywhere be paid instead, as two drachmas or denarii a head, to the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, and extended it to women, children and slaves.
events.detail: Ostraca receipts from Apollinopolis Magna (Edfu) in Egypt record payments by men, women and children. Domitian enforced it harshly, Suetonius recalling as a youth seeing a 90-year-old man stripped in court to see if he was circumcised. Nerva struck coins proclaiming FISCI IVDAICI CALVMNIA SVBLATA ('the false accusation of the Jewish treasury removed'), probably ending abuses rather than the tax. It identified Jews as a fiscal category and helped distinguish Christians from them.
scholarship: Heemstra, The Fiscus Judaicus and the Parting of the Ways (2010)

events.title: Triumph of Vespasian and Titus over Judaea
events.summary: Vespasian and Titus celebrated a joint triumph over Judaea, with Domitian riding beside them, displaying 700 picked captives, the Temple's golden table and seven-branched lampstand and a scroll of the Law. Simon bar Giora was executed at the climax.
events.detail: Josephus, an eyewitness, describes moving stages three or four storeys high depicting the war (BJ 7.123-157). The spoils were placed in the new Temple of Peace, the Law and the veils in the palace. The Arch of Titus on the Velia, erected after 81 by Domitian, shows the menorah carried in procession; a second arch in the Circus Maximus (81) claimed falsely that Titus was the first to capture Jerusalem. IVDAEA CAPTA coins circulated for a decade. The doors of Janus were closed.

events.title: Siege of Machaerus
events.summary: Lucilius Bassus, legate of Judaea, besieged Herod's fortress of Machaerus east of the Dead Sea. When a young rebel leader, Eleazar, was captured and prepared for crucifixion in view of the walls, the garrison surrendered in exchange for his life.
events.detail: Josephus says Machaerus was where John the Baptist was executed. Roman siege works (camps and a ramp) are still visible. Bassus also took Herodium and destroyed refugees in the forest of Jardes before dying in office; Flavius Silva succeeded him.

sides.losses: garrison released; 1,700 men of the lower town killed

battle.significance: Left Masada as the last rebel stronghold.

events.title: Annexation of Commagene and Flavian reorganisation of the East
events.summary: Accused by the Syrian governor Caesennius Paetus of plotting with Parthia, Antiochus IV of Commagene was driven out and his kingdom annexed to Syria. Lesser Armenia was also absorbed, and Vespasian combined Cappadocia and Galatia under a consular legate with legions on the upper Euphrates.
events.detail: Antiochus's sons fought a battle before fleeing to Parthia; the king retired to Sparta and then Rome, and his grandson Philopappus became an Athenian archon and Roman consul (his monument stands on the Mouseion hill in Athens). Legio XII Fulminata went to Melitene and XVI Flavia to Satala, creating for the first time a permanent legionary frontier facing Armenia. Emesa and other Syrian principalities were absorbed in the following years.

events.title: Siege of Masada
events.summary: Lucius Flavius Silva, with legio X Fretensis and auxiliaries, encircled Herod's desert fortress of Masada, held by about 960 Sicarii under Eleazar ben Yair, with a wall and eight camps, and built an assault ramp on the western side. When the wall was breached, Josephus says, the defenders killed their families and themselves the night before the final assault.
events.detail: Josephus gives Eleazar two long speeches advocating death over slavery and says only two women and five children survived by hiding in a cistern. Yigael Yadin's excavations (1963-65) uncovered the ramp, camps and circumvallation, Herod's palaces, a synagogue, scroll fragments and a group of ostraca with names, including 'ben Yair', which he interpreted as the lots described by Josephus, and a few skeletons. Masada became a symbol of Israeli national identity ('Masada shall not fall again'), and its narrative has been critically re-examined by Nachman Ben-Yehuda and others. The date depends on Silva's governorship: an inscription from Urbs Salvia makes 74 likely, though 73 is traditional.

sides.strength: Legio X Fretensis and auxiliaries, c. 8,000

battle.significance: Ended the First Jewish Revolt; later a national myth.

scholarship: Yadin, Masada (1966)
Ben-Yehuda, The Masada Myth (1995)
Eck, 'Die Eroberung von Masada und eine neue Inschrift des L. Flavius Silva Nonius Bassus', ZNW 60 (1969)
events.debate: Date (73 or 74); historicity of the mass suicide narrative.

events.title: Vespasian grants Latin rights to all Spain
events.summary: During his censorship with Titus (73-74), Vespasian granted the Latin right (ius Latii) to all communities of the Spanish provinces not already privileged, so that their annual magistrates acquired Roman citizenship, and Spanish towns were reorganised as Flavian municipia.
events.detail: Pliny says Vespasian 'tossed by the storms of the state' gave Latium to the whole of Spain. Bronze copies of the resulting municipal charter survive from Malaca and Salpensa (found 1851) and above all Irni (lex Irnitana, found in 1981 near El Saucejo, preserving about two-thirds of a standard Flavian municipal law in ten tablets), giving detailed rules on elections, councils, finance, manumission and civil jurisdiction. Over 350 Spanish communities may have benefited. The same censorship extended the pomerium (boundary stones of 75 survive) and adlected new senators, including provincials such as the father of Trajan.
events.locName: Irni (El Saucejo, Seville): find-spot of the lex Irnitana
scholarship: González and Crawford, 'The Lex Irnitana: a new copy of the Flavian municipal law', JRS 76 (1986)

events.title: Expulsion of philosophers and execution of Helvidius Priscus
events.summary: Vespasian expelled philosophers and astrologers from Rome (71) and, after repeated public defiance, exiled and then ordered the execution of the Stoic senator Helvidius Priscus, son-in-law of Thrasea Paetus, regretting it too late to recall the executioners.
events.detail: Helvidius refused to address Vespasian by any title but his private name and attacked hereditary succession. When the Cynic Demetrius insulted him, Vespasian is said to have replied that he did not kill a barking dog. The 'Stoic opposition', commemorated in Tacitus and Pliny, was less a philosophical programme than a code of senatorial independence. Helvidius's son was executed by Domitian in 93.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Peace
events.summary: Vespasian dedicated the Templum Pacis, a vast colonnaded garden-precinct beside the Forum of Augustus, built from Jewish war booty and housing the Temple treasures, a library and masterpieces of Greek painting and sculpture collected from Nero's palace.
events.detail: Pliny counted it among the most beautiful buildings in the world. The Severan Marble Plan of Rome (Forma Urbis) later hung on one of its walls; fragments survive. The precinct burned in 192, destroying among much else the books of Galen, who lamented the loss in his recently discovered treatise On the Avoidance of Grief.

events.title: Petillius Cerialis conquers the Brigantes
events.summary: After Venutius ousted his former wife, the pro-Roman queen Cartimandua, in 69, the Brigantes of northern England became hostile. Petillius Cerialis, as governor, waged a series of campaigns, founded the legionary fortress at Eboracum (York) for legio IX Hispana and annexed Brigantia.
events.detail: Tacitus says Cerialis fought many battles, some bloody, and conquered or ravaged much of Brigantia. The great earthworks at Stanwick in North Yorkshire, once thought to be Venutius's final stronghold, are now seen as an earlier royal centre. His successor Julius Frontinus subdued the Silures (74-77), building the fortress of Isca (Caerleon).

events.title: Josephus publishes the Jewish War
events.summary: Living in Rome as a Flavian client, Flavius Josephus published his seven-book Greek history of the Jewish revolt, revised from an earlier Aramaic version for the Jews of Mesopotamia. Vespasian and Titus endorsed it, Titus signing copies.
events.detail: The work presents the war as the fault of a small band of tyrants and brigands and of Roman procurators' misgovernment, exonerating the Flavians and the priestly aristocracy; Titus appears merciful. It is modelled on Thucydides and Polybius and uses Roman commentarii. Josephus later wrote the Jewish Antiquities (93/94), the Life and Against Apion. His works were preserved by Christians, partly because of the passages on Jesus, John the Baptist and James.

events.title: Pliny the Elder dedicates the Natural History
events.summary: Gaius Plinius Secundus dedicated his encyclopedic Natural History in 37 books to Titus, claiming in the preface to have assembled 20,000 facts from about 2,000 volumes by 100 principal authors.
events.detail: It covers cosmology, geography, anthropology, zoology, botany, medicine, metallurgy and art history, and is the main source for Greek painting and sculpture, Roman mining and countless technical details. His nephew describes his working method: read to while bathing and dining, taking notes always. The work circulated as an authority through the Middle Ages.

events.title: Death of Vespasian
events.summary: Vespasian died of fever and diarrhoea at his family's spa of Aquae Cutiliae near Reate, aged 69. Feeling death approach he joked 'Oh dear, I think I am becoming a god', and struggled to his feet, saying an emperor should die standing.
events.detail: He was the first emperor since Augustus to die naturally and be succeeded by his own son, Titus, who had been his colleague in tribunician power and censorship and praetorian prefect. His thrift (the tax on urine collected for fulling, 'money does not smell') restored finances drained by Nero and civil war; Suetonius says he estimated that 40,000 million sesterces were needed to set the state right.

events.title: Eruption of Vesuvius
events.summary: Vesuvius erupted catastrophically, burying Pompeii and Stabiae under pumice and ash and Herculaneum under pyroclastic flows. Pliny the Elder, commander of the fleet at Misenum, died at Stabiae while attempting a rescue; his nephew's two letters to Tacitus are the only eyewitness account.
events.detail: Pliny the Younger describes a column shaped like an umbrella pine (hence 'Plinian eruption'), rising perhaps 30 km, followed the next day by darkness and surges reaching Misenum. More than 1,100 bodies have been found at Pompeii (preserved as voids filled with plaster by Giuseppe Fiorelli from 1863) and over 300 skeletons in the boat-sheds of Herculaneum, discovered from 1980. The manuscripts give 'nonum Kal. Septembres' (24 August), but autumn fruits, braziers and a charcoal graffito dated 'XVI K Nov' (17 October) found in 2018 have persuaded many that the true date was 24 October. Titus sent senatorial commissioners and used the estates of victims without heirs for relief.
scholarship: Sigurdsson et al., 'The eruption of Vesuvius in A.D. 79', National Geographic Research 1 (1985)
Beard, Pompeii (2008)
events.debate: Date: 24 August (manuscript tradition) or 24 October (archaeological indicators, 2018 inscription).

events.title: Inauguration of the Colosseum
events.summary: Titus dedicated the Flavian Amphitheatre, begun by Vespasian on the site of Nero's lake, with 100 days of games in which 9,000 animals were killed and the arena was flooded for naval battles. Martial's Book of Spectacles celebrates them.
events.detail: The building, 189 by 156 m and about 48 m high, held perhaps 50,000 spectators, seated by rank, with 80 entrances and a velarium worked by sailors of the Misenum fleet. Géza Alföldy reconstructed the original dedicatory inscription from the dowel holes of its lost bronze letters: Vespasian 'ordered the new amphitheatre built from the spoils' (ex manubiis), meaning the booty of Jerusalem. Domitian completed the top storey and added the underground hypogeum. The same year a three-day fire burned the Capitol (again), the Pantheon and the Saepta, and a severe plague struck Rome.
scholarship: Alföldy, 'Eine Bauinschrift aus dem Colosseum', ZPE 109 (1995)
Hopkins and Beard, The Colosseum (2005)

events.title: Death of Titus
events.summary: Titus died of fever at the same Sabine villa as his father, aged 41, after a reign of just over two years in which he was remembered as 'the delight of the human race'. He reportedly said he regretted only one act, never explained.
events.detail: Rumours accused Domitian of hastening his death. Domitian deified him and built the Arch of Titus on the Velia, its inscription reading simply 'The Senate and Roman people to the deified Titus, son of the deified Vespasian'. Rabbinic legend (Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 56b) says a gnat entered his brain as punishment for destroying the Temple. His affair with the Jewish queen Berenice, whom he sent away on becoming emperor, fascinated later dramatists (Racine).

events.title: Domitian's campaign against the Chatti
events.summary: Domitian launched a surprise offensive from Mogontiacum against the Chatti, advancing Roman control into the Taunus and Wetterau and cutting 120 miles of military roads through the forest. He took the title Germanicus and celebrated a triumph.
events.detail: Frontinus, a participant, records the use of cleared limites to deny the enemy cover and compensation for crops destroyed by forts. The new line of watchtowers and forts became the nucleus of the upper German limes. Germania Superior and Inferior became regular provinces in these years, replacing the military districts. Hostile authors (Tacitus, Pliny, Dio) mocked the triumph as a fraud; archaeology supports real gains.

events.title: Battle of Mons Graupius
events.summary: Gnaeus Julius Agricola defeated a confederation of more than 30,000 Caledonians under Calgacus at Mons Graupius in north-east Scotland. He fought with 8,000 auxiliary infantry in the centre and 3,000 cavalry on the wings, keeping the legions in reserve before the camp; Tacitus reports 10,000 Caledonian and 360 Roman dead.
events.detail: Calgacus's pre-battle speech, invented by Tacitus, contains the most famous indictment of Roman imperialism: 'they make a desert and call it peace' (ubi solitudinem faciunt, pacem appellant). Batavian and Tungrian cohorts, fighting at close quarters with short swords, broke the Caledonian chariots and front ranks; the cavalry encircled the rest. Tacitus, Agricola's son-in-law, implies the victory completed the conquest of Britain, which Domitian then threw away. The site is unknown; proposals include Bennachie, Raedykes, Duncrub and Kempstone Hill, near the line of large marching camps.

sides.strength: 8,000 auxiliary infantry, 3,000 cavalry in the line; legions in reserve

battle.significance: Furthest northern victory of Roman arms in Britain; conquest of Scotland nonetheless abandoned within a few years.

scholarship: Hanson, Agricola and the Conquest of the North (1987)
Maxwell, A Battle Lost: Romans and Caledonians at Mons Graupius (1990)
events.debate: Year (83 or 84), site, and Tacitus's partiality.

events.title: Agricola's fleet circumnavigates Britain
events.summary: After Mons Graupius Agricola's fleet sailed round the north of Britain, subdued the Orkneys and sighted Thule, proving Britain to be an island. The year before, a cohort of Usipi, recently levied in Germany, had mutinied, stolen three ships and sailed round Britain by accident.
events.detail: The Usipi, killing a centurion and their instructors, drifted without pilots, were reduced to eating the weakest among them, were wrecked on the continent and sold as slaves by the Suebi and Frisii, some ending up on the Roman bank of the Rhine where their story became known. Tacitus presents the voyage as a final crowning of Agricola's governorship before his recall.

events.title: Domitian raises army pay and reforms the coinage
events.summary: Domitian raised legionary pay by a third, from 225 to 300 denarii a year, by adding a fourth instalment, the first increase since Augustus. In 82 he had restored the denarius to the Augustan silver standard, but rising costs forced a reduction in 85.
events.detail: Suetonius says the pay rise and the cost of building and games drove him to confiscations. Metallurgical analyses (Walker, Butcher and Ponting) confirm the sharp rise in fineness in 82 and the partial return in 85 to near-Neronian standards. The pay increase, together with the expanding army, became a permanent structural burden on imperial finances.
scholarship: Walker, The Metrology of the Roman Silver Coinage I (1976)
Speidel, 'Roman army pay scales', JRS 82 (1992)
events.debate: Whether the rise was in 83 or 84.

events.title: Dacian invasion of Moesia; death of Oppius Sabinus
events.summary: In winter 85/86 Dacians under their king (Duras or Diurpaneus, soon succeeded by Decebalus) crossed the frozen Danube into Moesia and killed the governor, Gaius Oppius Sabinus, with many of his troops.
events.detail: Domitian came to the Danube in person with the praetorian prefect Cornelius Fuscus, drove the invaders out and divided Moesia into Superior and Inferior (86). Jordanes, drawing on Dio, gives the Dacian perspective. The defeat began two decades of conflict culminating in Trajan's conquest.

battle.significance: Opened the Dacian wars of Domitian and Trajan.

events.title: Abandonment of the fortress at Inchtuthil
events.summary: The legionary fortress at Inchtuthil on the Tay, built for legio XX after Mons Graupius, was systematically dismantled before completion around 86-87, when legio II Adiutrix was withdrawn from Britain for the Danube wars. Ten tonnes of iron nails (about 875,000) were buried in a pit to keep them from the Caledonians.
events.detail: Excavated by Ian Richmond and J. K. St Joseph from 1952, Inchtuthil has the most complete plan of any legionary fortress: barracks, hospital, granaries, workshops, but no completed headquarters or commander's house. The latest coins are bronzes of 86. It is the archaeological counterpart of Tacitus's bitter phrase 'Britain was completely conquered and immediately let go' (Hist. 1.2).
scholarship: Pitts and St Joseph, Inchtuthil: The Roman Legionary Fortress (1985)

events.title: Defeat and death of Cornelius Fuscus
events.summary: The praetorian prefect Cornelius Fuscus led a Roman army across the Danube on a bridge of boats into Dacia and was killed with much of his force; a standard (or eagle) was lost, recovered by Trajan in 102.
events.detail: Juvenal mocks Fuscus as a man 'who studied war in his marble villa' and whose entrails were saved for Dacian vultures. Whether a legion (V Alaudae is the usual candidate) was destroyed is uncertain. The date may be 86 or 87. Decebalus, now king, emerged as a formidable opponent. The great funerary altar at Adamclisi, listing some 3,800 Roman dead, is sometimes attributed to this disaster rather than to Trajan's war.

sides.strength: Several legions or vexillations with praetorians

battle.significance: Made Decebalus Rome's most dangerous enemy on the Danube.

events.debate: Date (86/87), site, and whether a legion was annihilated.

events.title: Domitian's Secular Games
events.summary: Domitian celebrated Secular Games in 88, reckoning from Augustus's games of 17 BC rather than following Claudius's anniversary cycle of 47. Tacitus took part as praetor and member of the quindecimviri sacris faciundis.
events.detail: Tacitus mentions his role in passing (Ann. 11.11), one of the few autobiographical facts we have about him. The competing calculations (Augustan 110-year saecula, Claudian centenary of the city) show how the antiquarian calendar was manipulated for political ends.

events.title: Battle of Tapae (88)
events.summary: Lucius Tettius Julianus, governor of Upper Moesia, invaded Dacia and defeated Decebalus near Tapae, the pass leading to the Dacian heartland. Decebalus's lieutenant Vezinas survived by lying among the dead.
events.detail: Dio says Decebalus, fearing a Roman advance on his capital, had trees felled and dressed in armour so that the Romans would take them for soldiers. Julianus made his soldiers inscribe their own and their centurions' names on their shields to encourage bravery. The victory was not followed up because of the Saturninus revolt and war with the Suebi.

battle.significance: Restored Roman prestige and led to a negotiated peace.

events.title: Revolt of Antonius Saturninus
events.summary: On 1 January 89 Lucius Antonius Saturninus, governor of upper Germany, was proclaimed emperor by the two legions at Mogontiacum, using the soldiers' savings in the camp bank. A sudden thaw on the Rhine prevented his Chattan allies from crossing, and Aulus Bucius Lappius Maximus crushed him within weeks.
events.detail: Lappius burned Saturninus's correspondence to prevent a witch-hunt, but Domitian's suspicion deepened. Trajan, then legate of legio VII Gemina in Spain, marched to the Rhine too late to fight. Domitian thereafter forbade two legions sharing a camp and limited soldiers' deposits to 1,000 sesterces. The episode marks the start of the 'terror' of Domitian's later years in the hostile tradition.

events.title: Peace with Decebalus
events.summary: Facing war with the Marcomanni and Quadi, Domitian made peace with Decebalus, whose brother Diegis came to receive a diadem as a client king. Rome paid Decebalus an annual subsidy and lent him engineers and craftsmen.
events.detail: Domitian then celebrated a double triumph over the Chatti and Dacians, which hostile writers mocked. Dio says Decebalus used Roman artisans to build up his fortifications in the Orăștie mountains, a grievance Trajan later exploited. Modern historians view the peace as a sensible arrangement that freed troops for the more urgent Suebic-Sarmatian front.

events.title: Execution of the Vestal Cornelia
events.summary: Domitian, as pontifex maximus, condemned the senior Vestal Cornelia for unchastity and had her buried alive in the ancient manner; her alleged lovers were beaten to death with rods in the Comitium.
events.detail: Pliny the Younger describes her protesting her innocence as she was led to the underground chamber, adjusting her robe so as to descend with dignity. Earlier (c. 83) the Oculatae sisters and Varronilla had been allowed to choose their deaths. Domitian's revival of archaic religious penalties fits his self-image as restorer of morals and censor perpetuus (from 85).
events.locName: Rome (Campus Sceleratus by the Colline Gate)

events.title: Domitian's vine edict
events.summary: After an abundant vintage coincided with a grain shortage, Domitian forbade the planting of new vines in Italy and ordered half the vineyards in the provinces to be cut down. The edict was not enforced and was suspended, according to Philostratus, after an embassy from Asia led by the sophist Scopelian.
events.detail: Modern interpretations range from protection of Italian wine producers to concern for grain supply. The measure was formally lifted only by Probus (c. 280). It is a rare example of an imperial attempt at agricultural regulation across the empire.

events.title: Destruction of legio XXI Rapax
events.summary: The Sarmatian Iazyges, with Suebic allies, invaded Pannonia and destroyed a legion with its legate, almost certainly XXI Rapax, which disappears from the record at this time. Domitian took the field himself for eight months.
events.detail: Suetonius mentions 'a legion slaughtered with its legate' in the Sarmatian war. Domitian celebrated only an ovatio in January 93, dedicating a laurel wreath to Capitoline Jupiter. Pannonia's garrison was reinforced, and Aquincum, Brigetio and Vindobona developed as legionary bases in the following years.

battle.significance: Shifted Rome's military centre of gravity to the middle Danube.

events.title: Dedication of Domitian's Palatine palace
events.summary: Domitian's architect Rabirius completed the great palace on the Palatine, comprising the official Domus Flavia with its throne room (Aula Regia) and state dining hall, and the private Domus Augustana with its sunken peristyle and 'stadium' garden.
events.detail: Statius (Silvae 4.2) describes a banquet in the dining hall, where the emperor's presence is likened to Jupiter's. The palace remained the emperors' residence for three centuries and gave the word 'palace' (from Palatium) to European languages. Martial praises Rabirius's genius.

events.title: Vindolanda writing tablets
events.summary: Waterlogged deposits at the fort of Vindolanda, south of the later Hadrian's Wall, have yielded since 1973 over a thousand thin wooden leaf tablets written in ink, mostly from about 92-120: military reports, accounts and private letters of soldiers, officers and their families.
events.detail: Highlights include a strength report of the First Cohort of Tungrians showing 752 men on the books but only 296 present, the rest seconded elsewhere (Tab. Vindol. II 154); a birthday invitation from Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, the wife of the Batavian prefect Flavius Cerialis, with a postscript in Severa's own hand, the earliest known Latin writing by a woman (II 291); a memorandum referring dismissively to 'Brittunculi', 'wretched little Britons' (II 164); and requests for socks, underpants and beer. They transformed knowledge of everyday military life, literacy and the Latin of the frontier.
scholarship: Bowman and Thomas, The Vindolanda Writing-Tablets (Tabulae Vindolandenses II, 1994)
Bowman, Life and Letters on the Roman Frontier (1994)

events.title: The terror of 93: executions of senators and expulsion of philosophers
events.summary: After Agricola's death in August 93, Domitian had the senators Herennius Senecio and Arulenus Rusticus executed for writing eulogies of Helvidius Priscus and Thrasea Paetus, and the younger Helvidius for an allegedly satirical farce. Their books were burned in the Forum, and philosophers were expelled from Rome and Italy.
events.detail: Tacitus, who was absent from Rome, opens the Agricola with the bitter claim that the Senate had given proof of extreme servitude and that Rome had lost even the memory of free speech. Pliny the Younger, praetor that year, claims (perhaps exaggerating) to have been in danger himself. Epictetus left for Nicopolis in Epirus, where his lectures were recorded by Arrian. The women Arria and Fannia were exiled.

events.title: Execution of Flavius Clemens
events.summary: Domitian had his cousin Titus Flavius Clemens, consul with him in 95 and father of the boys he had designated as heirs, executed for 'atheism', and exiled Clemens's wife Flavia Domitilla. Dio says many others who had 'drifted into Jewish ways' were condemned.
events.detail: Eusebius makes Domitilla a Christian, exiled to Pontia; the Catacomb of Domitilla in Rome is on land associated with her family. Whether the charge reflects Judaising, Christianity or simply dynastic fear is disputed. The execution alarmed the palace staff; Domitilla's steward Stephanus was among Domitian's assassins months later.
events.debate: Jewish or Christian sympathies of Clemens and Domitilla.

events.title: Assassination of Domitian
events.summary: Domitian was stabbed to death in his bedroom by a palace conspiracy including his chamberlain Parthenius and Stephanus, steward of the exiled Domitilla, who had worn a bandage for days to hide a dagger. Both praetorian prefects and perhaps the empress Domitia knew of the plot.
events.detail: Domitian, aged 44, fought back fiercely. The Senate rejoiced, ordered his images destroyed and his name erased from inscriptions (damnatio memoriae), and immediately recognised Marcus Cocceius Nerva. The soldiers, who had loved Domitian for his pay rise, were angry. Philostratus tells that Apollonius of Tyana, lecturing at Ephesus, saw the murder in a vision at the moment it happened. Suetonius ends his Twelve Caesars with Domitian's death and the prophecy of better times.
